```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false

library(tidyverse)
library(here)
library(knitr)
library(scales)
library(patchwork)
library(MASS)
library(nnet)

# MASS::select masks dplyr's, and we want dplyr's everywhere below
select <- dplyr::select

knitr::opts_chunk$set(dev = "ragg_png")

# CASA palette, stated explicitly so the deck does not depend on casaviz
casa_purple <- "#4E3C56"
casa_teal   <- "#2E6260"
casa_yellow <- "#F9DD73"
casa_pink   <- "#E16FCA"
casa_green  <- "#9DBB65"
casa_red    <- "#C94C4C"
casa_cols   <- c("#2E6260", "#658E62", "#9DBB65", "#E7D870",
                 "#F3C486", "#E993AC", "#8F5289", "#4E3C56")

theme_set(theme_minimal(base_size = 16))

base_path <- here("sessions", "L6_data", "Performancetables_130242", "2022-2023")

# The DfE publishes suppressed / not-applicable values as codes, not blanks
na_all <- c("", "NA", "SUPP", "NP", "NE", "SP", "SN", "LOWCOV", "NEW", "SUPPMAT")

# Every file is keyed on URN. The LA and national summary rows carry no URN,
# and because dplyr joins NA to NA they would duplicate rows as well as not
# being schools - so they go before anything else happens.
read_dfe <- function(f) {
  suppressWarnings(
    read_csv(file.path(base_path, f), na = na_all, show_col_types = FALSE)
  ) |>
    mutate(URN = as.character(URN)) |>
    filter(!is.na(URN))
}

ks4 <- read_dfe("england_ks4final.csv") |>
  select(URN, ATT8SCR, P8MEA, TPUP, PTFSM6CLA1A, TFSM6CLA1A, PTEALGRP2, PTPRIORHI) |>
  mutate(across(-URN, ~ parse_number(as.character(.x))))

absence <- read_dfe("england_abs.csv") |>
  distinct(URN, .keep_all = TRUE) |>
  select(URN, PERCTOT, PPERSABS10) |>
  mutate(across(-URN, ~ parse_number(as.character(.x))))

school_info <- read_dfe("england_school_information.csv") |>
  select(URN, SCHNAME, LANAME, MINORGROUP, OFSTEDRATING, OFSTEDLASTINSP)

destinations <- read_dfe("england_ks4-pupdest.csv") |>
  distinct(URN, .keep_all = TRUE) |>
  select(URN, COHORT, OVERALL_DEST) |>
  mutate(across(-URN, ~ parse_number(as.character(.x))))

# Mainstream secondaries with an Ofsted judgement. Ofsted's five published
# grades collapse to four analytical ones: "serious weaknesses" and "special
# measures" are both categories of inadequate in Ofsted's own scheme, and
# separately they are far too small to model.
schools <- ks4 |>
  inner_join(absence, by = "URN") |>
  inner_join(school_info, by = "URN") |>
  filter(MINORGROUP %in% c("Academy", "Maintained school"),
         OFSTEDRATING %in% c("Outstanding", "Good", "Requires improvement",
                             "Serious Weaknesses", "Special Measures")) |>
  mutate(
    rating4 = case_when(
      OFSTEDRATING == "Outstanding"           ~ "Outstanding",
      OFSTEDRATING == "Good"                  ~ "Good",
      OFSTEDRATING == "Requires improvement"  ~ "Requires improvement",
      TRUE                                    ~ "Inadequate"),
    rating4 = factor(rating4,
                     levels = c("Inadequate", "Requires improvement",
                                "Good", "Outstanding"),
                     ordered = TRUE),
    below_good  = as.integer(rating4 %in% c("Inadequate", "Requires improvement")),
    outstanding = as.integer(rating4 == "Outstanding"),
    insp_year   = suppressWarnings(as.integer(substr(OFSTEDLASTINSP, 7, 10)))
  )

model_data <- schools |>
  drop_na(P8MEA, PTFSM6CLA1A, PERCTOT, PPERSABS10, TPUP, PTPRIORHI)

# One split, used by every classification model in the deck
set.seed(42)
train_idx <- sample(nrow(model_data), floor(0.7 * nrow(model_data)))
train <- model_data[train_idx, ]
test  <- model_data[-train_idx, ]

# AUC by the rank identity, so the deck needs no extra package
auc_of <- function(scores, actual) {
  r  <- rank(scores)
  n1 <- sum(actual == 1); n0 <- sum(actual == 0)
  (sum(r[actual == 1]) - n1 * (n1 + 1) / 2) / (n1 * n0)
}

# Every model below spells its formula out in full rather than sharing one
# object. More typing, but the code on the slide is then exactly the code that
# runs, which matters more in a teaching deck than staying DRY.
```

## Last time {transition="convex-in none-out" transition-speed="fast"}

-   We met the **Generalised Linear Model** — one framework, three moving
    parts: a distribution, a linear predictor, and a **link function**
-   We spent the session on **logistic regression**, because once you can read
    an odds ratio the rest of the family follows
-   And we left three outcome types on the table. This session picks up the
    biggest of them: **counts**

## This session {transition="convex-in none-out" transition-speed="fast"}

::: {.incremental}
-   **$E[y]$** — the notation the count models are written in, and why it is
    nothing new
-   **Poisson regression** for counts, and how to read a rate ratio
-   **Offsets** — the thing that turns a model of counts into a model of
    *rates*, which is almost always what you actually wanted
-   **Overdispersion**, and the **negative binomial** model that deals with it
-   **Proportions** — *x out of n* — which turn out to be a binomial problem
    in disguise
:::

. . .

Same dataset, same schools. The only thing changing is what we put on the
left-hand side.

# First, a word on notation {background-color="#4e3c56"}
## A quick word on $E[y]$ {.smaller transition="convex-in none-out" transition-speed="fast"}

With GLMs there is an $E$ in most of the equations. **$E$ is for
expectation**, and $E[y_i]$ reads *"the expected value of y for school i"*.

::: incremental
-   It is essentially **an average** — but a theoretical one. Your sample
    mean is a fact about the 3,000 schools you happen to have; an expected
    value is a fact about the **process that produced them**
-   **"Expected" is a poor name.** It need not be a value you could ever
    observe — the expected value of a dice roll is 3.5, and the expected
    number of children per family is about 1.8
-   **The little $i$ matters.** $E[y_i]$ is *that school's own* expected
    value, and it depends on that school's predictors. There are thousands of
    them, one per school — not a single average across the dataset
:::

## You have been using it all along {.smaller transition="convex-in none-out" transition-speed="fast"}

Ordinary regression, exactly as we wrote it in Vol 1:

$$y_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1x_i + \epsilon_i$$

. . .

The errors average out to zero. So take the average of both sides, and the
error term disappears:

$$E[y_i] = \beta_0 + \beta_1x_i$$

. . .

::: {style="font-size: 0.95em"}
**That is the line you have been drawing through scatter plots since week 5.**
-   A regression line was never an exact school prediction
—   It is a prediction of what the *average* school like it does - this is the expected value
:::

. . .

::: {style="background-color:#2e6260; color:white; padding:8px; border-radius:5px; font-size:0.88em;"}
So $\log(E[y_i])$ is **not anything new or different**. Just more formalised in the GLM equation.
:::

## The same model, three times {.smaller transition="convex-in none-out" transition-speed="fast"}

Written out in full, with the **right-hand side identical every time**. Only
the left changes.

::: {style="font-size: 0.95em"}
**Ordinary regression** — the outcome goes in as it is:

$$y_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1x_1 + \beta_2x_2 + \dots + \epsilon_i$$
:::

. . .

::: {style="font-size: 0.95em"}
**Logistic regression** — last session. The *probability* goes in, through the
logit:

$$\log\!\left(\frac{p_i}{1-p_i}\right) = \beta_0 + \beta_1x_1 + \beta_2x_2 + \dots$$
:::

. . .

::: {style="font-size: 0.95em"}
**Poisson regression** — today. The *expected count* goes in, through a log:

$$\log\big(E[y_i]\big) = \beta_0 + \beta_1x_1 + \beta_2x_2 + \dots$$
:::

. . .

::: {style="background-color:#2e6260; color:white; padding:9px; border-radius:5px; font-size:0.86em;"}
Notice what is **missing** from the bottom two: the $\epsilon$. OLS adds an
error term on the end; a GLM does not, because the randomness is already
described by the distribution you chose. **That is the swap** — an error term
for a distribution.
:::

# Counting things {background-color="#4e3c56"}

## A different kind of outcome {transition="convex-in none-out" transition-speed="fast"}

Let's change the question and move up a level.

::: {style="font-size: 1.05em"}
*How many below-Good schools does each local authority have?*
:::

::: incremental
- That is a **count**: 0, 1, 2, 3... never negative, never fractional
- Most LAs have a few; some have none at all; a couple have a lot
- A straight line will happily predict minus two struggling schools,
  which is not a thing
:::

## What counts look like {transition="convex-in none-out" transition-speed="fast"}

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| fig-width: 11
#| fig-height: 4.2
#| out-width: 95%

la <- schools |>
  group_by(LANAME) |>
  summarise(n_schools = n(),
            n_below   = sum(below_good),
            mean_fsm  = mean(PTFSM6CLA1A, na.rm = TRUE),
            mean_abs  = mean(PERCTOT, na.rm = TRUE),
            .groups = "drop") |>
  filter(n_schools >= 5)

ggplot(la, aes(n_below)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 1, fill = casa_teal, colour = "white") +
  labs(x = "Schools rated below Good", y = "Local authorities",
       title = sprintf("%d local authorities; mean %.2f, variance %.2f",
                       nrow(la), mean(la$n_below), var(la$n_below)))
```

::: {style="font-size: 0.85em"}
Discrete, non-negative, right-skewed, with a pile-up at the low end -
**`r sum(la$n_below == 0)`** LAs have no below-Good schools at all. This
is a Poisson-shaped problem, exactly as week 1 described.
:::

## But first - counts or rates? {transition="convex-in none-out" transition-speed="fast"}

```{r}
#| label: offset-motivate
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false
pick <- la |>
  filter(LANAME %in% c("Lancashire", "Bury")) |>
  arrange(desc(n_schools)) |>
  transmute(`Local authority` = LANAME,
            `Secondary schools` = n_schools,
            `Rated below Good` = n_below,
            `As a share` = sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * n_below / n_schools))
knitr::kable(pick, align = "lrrr")
```

. . .

::: {style="font-size: 0.95em"}
**On the raw count, Lancashire looks nearly four times worse.** On the share,
Bury is the one in trouble.

A count on its own tells you very little, because it depends on how many
chances there were to begin with. Lancashire has six times as many schools, so
it would take more below-Good ones even if nothing were wrong.
:::

## So why not just divide? {.smaller transition="convex-in none-out" transition-speed="fast"}

The obvious move is to model the share — `n_below / n_schools` — and be done
with it. Two reasons not to:

::: incremental
-   **Poisson describes whole numbers.** `22/79 = 0.28` is not a count of
    anything. We would be using a distribution for something it does not
    describe
-   **Dividing throws away how much evidence you have.** Bury's 46% rests on
    **13** schools. Lancashire's 28% rests on **79**. We should be far more
    confident about Lancashire — but once both are just "a percentage", the
    model can no longer tell them apart
:::

. . .

::: {style="font-size: 0.95em"}
An **offset** gets us both: the outcome stays a genuine count, so Poisson
still applies and the sample sizes still count for something — but the model
does the dividing internally.
:::

## What an offset actually is {.smaller transition="convex-in none-out" transition-speed="fast"}

Three lines of algebra, and nothing clever happens in any of them.

::: {style="font-size: 0.95em"}
**1. What we actually want to model** — a rate, not a count:

$$\log\left(\frac{\text{expected count}}{\text{number of schools}}\right) = \beta_0 + \beta_1x$$

**2. The log of a ratio is a difference of logs** — ordinary school algebra:

$$\log(\text{expected count}) - \log(\text{number of schools}) = \beta_0 + \beta_1x$$

**3. Move that term across to the other side:**

$$\log(\text{expected count}) = \beta_0 + \beta_1x + \log(\text{number of schools})$$

That final term — $\log(\text{number of schools})$ — **is the offset**.
:::

. . .

::: {style="font-size: 0.95em"}
So an offset is just **a division, rewritten as an addition** so it can sit
inside a model that works on the log scale. In R that is
`offset(log(n_schools))`.
:::

## Fixed, not estimated {.smaller transition="convex-in none-out" transition-speed="fast"}

Look at line 3 again. Every other term on the right gets a $\beta$ in front of
it that the model **chooses**. The offset does not — it is stuck there with a
coefficient of exactly **1**, because that is how it arrived.

. . .

::: {style="font-size: 0.95em"}
In plain words, we are **telling** the model something rather than asking it:

> *Twice as many schools, twice as many below-Good ones expected, all else
> being equal.*

That is a claim about arithmetic, not about education policy, so we spend no
parameter finding it out.
:::

. . .

```{r}
#| label: offset-vs-estimated
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false
est_m <- glm(n_below ~ mean_abs + log(n_schools), data = la, family = poisson)
ci    <- confint.default(est_m)["log(n_schools)", ]
```

::: {style="background-color:#2e6260; color:white; padding:10px; border-radius:5px; font-size:0.86em;"}
**Is that a fair thing to assume?** Put `log(n_schools)` in as an ordinary
predictor and let the model estimate it instead. It comes back with
**`r sprintf("%.2f", coef(est_m)["log(n_schools)"])`**, with a 95% interval of
`r sprintf("%.2f", ci[1])` to `r sprintf("%.2f", ci[2])` — 1 sits comfortably
inside it. The assumption holds, and fixing it saves us a parameter.

**Always worth checking.** If that interval had excluded 1, the offset would
have been the wrong tool.
:::
## Running a Poisson model {transition="convex-in none-out" transition-speed="fast"}

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| message: false
#| warning: false
pois <- glm(n_below ~ mean_fsm + mean_abs + offset(log(n_schools)),
            data = la, family = poisson)
```

```{r}
#| echo: false
pc <- summary(pois)$coefficients
tibble(
  Term = c("(Intercept)", "Mean % disadvantaged", "Mean % absence"),
  Coefficient = round(pc[, 1], 4),
  `Rate ratio` = round(exp(pc[, 1]), 3),
  `p` = ifelse(pc[, 4] < 0.001, "<0.001", as.character(round(pc[, 4], 3)))
) |> kable()
```

. . .

::: {style="font-size: 0.9em"}
The link function here is $\log$, so exponentiating gives a **rate
ratio**. And note the result: once average absence is in the model,
**average disadvantage adds nothing detectable** - a confounding story
of exactly the kind we met in week 6.
:::

## Checking the Poisson assumption {transition="convex-in none-out" transition-speed="fast"}

The Poisson distribution assumes something quite strong: that the
**variance equals the mean**. Real data often disagrees.

```{r}
#| echo: true
dispersion <- pois$deviance / pois$df.residual
dispersion
```

. . .

::: {style="font-size: 0.95em"}
A value near **1** means the assumption holds. Much above 1 means
**overdispersion** - the data are more variable than Poisson allows,
your standard errors are too small, and you will think results are
significant when they are not.

Here we get **`r sprintf("%.2f", dispersion)`**, which is mild. So
Poisson is adequate - but we should check rather than assume.
:::

## When it is not adequate {transition="convex-in none-out" transition-speed="fast"}

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false
nb <- MASS::glm.nb(n_below ~ mean_fsm + mean_abs + offset(log(n_schools)), data = la)

tibble(
  Model = c("Poisson", "Negative binomial"),
  AIC = round(c(AIC(pois), AIC(nb))),
  `SE on absence` = sprintf("%.4f", c(summary(pois)$coefficients["mean_abs", 2],
                                      summary(nb)$coefficients["mean_abs", 2]))
) |> kable()
```

- The **negative binomial** is the Poisson's more forgiving cousin - it
  adds a parameter that lets the variance exceed the mean
- This is exactly the distribution we met in week 1, and this is what it
  is for
- Here the two models are essentially tied, so we keep the simpler one

. . .

**Fit the Poisson, check the dispersion, escalate only if you need to.**

## The fun bit: who beats their own odds? {transition="convex-in none-out" transition-speed="fast"}

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| fig-width: 11
#| fig-height: 4.4
#| out-width: 95%

la <- la |>
  mutate(expected = fitted(pois),
         resid    = (n_below - expected) / sqrt(expected))

plot_la <- bind_rows(
  la |> slice_max(resid, n = 6) |> mutate(grp = "More than expected"),
  la |> slice_min(resid, n = 6) |> mutate(grp = "Fewer than expected")
)

plot_la |>
  pivot_longer(c(n_below, expected), names_to = "what", values_to = "val") |>
  mutate(what = recode(what, n_below = "Observed", expected = "Model expects")) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = val, y = fct_reorder(LANAME, resid), colour = what)) +
  geom_line(aes(group = LANAME), colour = "grey70", linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point(size = 3.4) +
  facet_wrap(~grp, scales = "free_y") +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("Observed" = casa_red, "Model expects" = casa_teal),
                      name = NULL) +
  labs(x = "Schools rated below Good", y = NULL,
       title = "Where the model is wrong, and in which direction") +
  theme(legend.position = "top")
```

::: {style="font-size: 0.8em"}
Given their intake, some LAs have far **more** struggling schools than
expected and some far **fewer**. The residuals of a count model are not
a diagnostic afterthought here - they are the finding.
:::

# One more outcome type {background-color="#4e3c56"}

## Proportions out of a known total {transition="convex-in none-out" transition-speed="fast"}

Back down to school level, and to a file we have not touched yet: **what
happens to pupils after Year 11?**

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false
dest <- destinations |>
  inner_join(schools, by = "URN") |>
  filter(!is.na(COHORT), COHORT > 0, !is.na(OVERALL_DEST), !is.na(PTFSM6CLA1A)) |>
  mutate(not_sust = COHORT - OVERALL_DEST,
         prop     = OVERALL_DEST / COHORT) |>
  filter(not_sust >= 0)

tibble(
  ` ` = c("Schools", "Median cohort", "Median % sustaining a destination",
          "Schools at exactly 100%"),
  Value = c(comma(nrow(dest)), comma(median(dest$COHORT)),
            sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * median(dest$prop)),
            sprintf("%d (%.1f%%)", sum(dest$prop == 1), 100 * mean(dest$prop == 1)))
) |> kable()
```

- Each school gives us "**x** of **n** pupils went on to education,
  employment or training"
- That is not really a percentage - it is a **count out of a known
  total**, which is exactly what the binomial distribution describes

## Modelling it properly {transition="convex-in none-out" transition-speed="fast"}

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| message: false
#| warning: false
dest_glm <- glm(cbind(OVERALL_DEST, not_sust) ~ PTFSM6CLA1A,
                data = dest, family = binomial)
```

```{r}
#| echo: false
or10 <- exp(coef(dest_glm)["PTFSM6CLA1A"] * 10)
```

::: {style="font-size: 1.05em"}
Note the `cbind()` - we hand the model **successes and failures**, not a
proportion, so it knows a school of 30 carries less weight than a school
of 300.
:::

. . .

::: {style="font-size: 1.05em"}
**Every 10 percentage points more disadvantage is associated with a
`r sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * (1 - or10))` fall in the odds of a pupil
sustaining a destination.**
:::

## Does it matter? Compare the predictions {transition="convex-in none-out" transition-speed="fast"}

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| fig-width: 11
#| fig-height: 4.3
#| out-width: 95%

dest_ols <- lm(I(prop * 100) ~ PTFSM6CLA1A, data = dest)
gd <- tibble(PTFSM6CLA1A = seq(0, 100, length.out = 200))
gd$OLS <- predict(dest_ols, newdata = gd)
gd$GLM <- 100 * predict(dest_glm, newdata = gd, type = "response")

ggplot() +
  geom_point(data = dest, aes(PTFSM6CLA1A, 100 * prop),
             alpha = 0.10, colour = casa_purple, size = 0.8) +
  geom_line(data = gd, aes(PTFSM6CLA1A, OLS, colour = "Straight line (OLS)"), linewidth = 1.3) +
  geom_line(data = gd, aes(PTFSM6CLA1A, GLM, colour = "Binomial GLM"), linewidth = 1.3) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("Straight line (OLS)" = casa_red,
                                 "Binomial GLM" = casa_teal), name = NULL) +
  labs(x = "% disadvantaged pupils", y = "% sustaining a destination",
       title = "Same data, two models") +
  theme(legend.position = "top")
```

::: {style="font-size: 0.85em"}
They agree almost exactly through the middle and **diverge at the top
end** - the schools policy cares about most. Here OLS is not obviously
broken. It is quietly wrong at the edges, and **nothing in its output
tells you so**.
:::

## And check the dispersion again {transition="convex-in none-out" transition-speed="fast"}

```{r}
#| echo: false
disp_dest <- dest_glm$deviance / dest_glm$df.residual
tibble(
  Model = c("LA below-Good counts (Poisson)", "Destinations (binomial)"),
  Dispersion = sprintf("%.2f", c(dispersion, disp_dest)),
  Verdict = c("Mild - Poisson is fine",
              "Overdispersed - use quasibinomial")
) |> kable()
```

. . .

- **Two models, two different answers.** The check is not a formality
  you tick off
- For the destinations model, switching to `family = quasibinomial`
  widens the standard errors by about 60% - the coefficients are
  unchanged, but our confidence in them was overstated


# Wrapping up {background-color="#4e3c56"}

## The family, in one slide {.smaller transition="convex-in none-out" transition-speed="fast"}

| Outcome | `family =` | Link | Interpret coefficients as |
|------------------|------------------|------------------|------------------|
| Continuous | `gaussian` | identity | Units of y per unit of x |
| Yes / no | `binomial` | logit | Odds ratios |
| **x out of n** | `binomial` | logit | Odds ratios |
| Ordered categories | `MASS::polr()` | logit | Odds of being in a higher category |
| Unordered categories | `nnet::multinom()` | logit | Odds vs a reference category |
| **Count** | `poisson` | log | **Rate ratios** |
| **Overdispersed count** | `MASS::glm.nb()` | log | **Rate ratios** |

. . .

**One framework.** Change the family, change the link, and everything you
learned about building and interpreting a linear model still applies.

## Conclusions {.smaller transition="convex-in none-out" transition-speed="fast"}

::: {.incremental}
-   A **count** is not a continuous number. It cannot go negative, it comes in
    whole units, and its variance grows with its mean — so it gets a log link
    and a Poisson distribution
-   **An offset is a division in disguise.** It turns counts into rates, and
    it is the single most commonly forgotten piece of a count model
-   **Always check the dispersion.** Much above 1 and your standard errors are
    too small, which means significance you have not earned
-   A **proportion out of a known total** is a binomial, not a percentage to
    be modelled with OLS — `cbind(successes, failures)` keeps the sample sizes
    in the model where they belong
:::

. . .

::: {style="background-color:#2e6260; color:white; padding:9px; border-radius:5px; font-size:0.88em;"}
And the thread running through both sessions: **look at your outcome variable
before you choose a model.** Week 1's data types were never an academic
exercise — they decide what you are allowed to do.
:::

## Today's Practical {transition="convex-in none-out" transition-speed="fast"}

-   Fitting Poisson models to the schools data, with and without an offset,
    and seeing what the offset changes
-   Checking dispersion, and deciding whether you need the negative binomial
-   Reading **rate ratios** out loud in plain English — the same skill as
    odds ratios, one family along
